newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan leader begins 4th year amid coup rumors.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan leader begins 4th year amid coup rumors.

text.p: Venezuela's Rafael Caldera, Latin America's oldest president, began his fourth year in power on Monday facing seasonal coup rumours.
Interior Minister Jose Guillermo Andueza emphatically denied the rumours, which continued a four-year tradition marking a Feb. 4, 1992 attempted coup by Gen. Hugo Cesar Chavez.
"There is no coup, nor will there be one," Andueza told reporters. The army "is monolithically united behind the President of the Republic."

Venezuela is emerging from three years of unprecedented recession, and the buzz comes after a month of labour unrest over falling living standards that political sources say has spread to the military.

"The (military's) uneasiness stems from the conduct of some high placed people who are divorced from the duties of military life," said retired Vice-Admiral Gruber Odreman, who led a second attempted coup on Nov. 27, 1992.
The left-leaning Chavez, who intends to run for the presidency in December 1998, said he knew of two coup plots.
One, he said in an interview published on Sunday, would potentially be headed by Caldera's son-in-law and head of the Presidential Guard of Honour, Gen. Ruben Rojas Perez.
Asked to comment, Rojas told Reuters: "I don't propagate rumours."
Caldera, 81, now serving his second presidential term 20 years after his first, has seen his popularity plummet since he took office three years ago.
Paradoxically, it was Chavez's attempted coup that resuscitated what many considered a slumbering political career for Caldera.
Days after Chavez failed to storm the Presidential Palace, national television broadcast Caldera telling Congress one could not expect people to defend democracy if they were starving.
Viewed as the incorruptible grandfather of Venezuelan politics, Caldera went on to assume the presidency on Feb. 2, 1994 with a populist platform and a 74 percent approval rating.
That rating has slipped to 20 after triple digit inflation last year laid waste to wages, leaving an estimated eight out of ten Venezuelans living in poverty.
Caldera's woes are buttressed by an astrologer's prediction he will be forced from office this year.

"The planet's positions during this new month (February) point towards a combative and difficult time," said Jose Bernando Gomez, a respected astrologer who was detained by police in October after predicting Caldera would no longer be in power after June 8.
